Social conference at Matignon: the government aims for a minimum wage above 1,500 euros net, unions want up to 150 more

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu brings unions and employers together at Matignon on Monday 9 November to discuss the minimum wage (Smic) and pay, four days after a day of protest that drew 575,000 people according to the Interior Ministry. The net Smic is 1,477.93 euros: the executive aims for 1,500, the CFDT asks for 100 euros more, the CGT 150 [1][3][6].

The social conference takes place on Monday 9 November at Matignon, with the State, the unions and employers; on the agenda: the Smic, sector-level minimum wages and pay negotiations in companies [1].

Sébastien Lecornu announced it on Thursday 5 November, the day of a national day of action that brought out 575,000 people in 193 street actions, including 65,000 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry; the provisional 6 p.m. tally counted 448 arrests and 53 law-enforcement officers injured [1][6].
The Smic stands at 1,477.93 euros net per month. Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou considers it "important" to try to "cross the bar" of 1,500 euros net, only about twenty euros more [1][3].

Farandou also says the government is studying bringing forward the increase to 1 December; an "exceptional" boost is "not taboo", and a decree is ready to encourage companies to raise their sector minimums up to the Smic level [3][9].

The unions are asking for much more, according to AFP: 100 euros net per month for the CFDT of Marylise Léon, 10% (about 150 euros net) for the CGT of Sophie Binet, a Smic of 2,000 euros for Force Ouvrière [1][4].
On the employers' side, the Medef says: "For the moment, we have no concrete opening on payroll-tax relief" [1].
Faced with Jean-Luc Mélenchon's proposal of a Smic at 1,700 euros net, Farandou argues it would destroy more than 230,000 jobs; this is the minister's estimate, not an official figure [3].

Key point: the government is looking for a gesture on pay that calms the street without raising the cost of labour, and that is exactly where unions and employers part ways: the former want pay rises, the Medef refuses to discuss rises without lower payroll charges [1][3].

A "coup de pouce" (boost) to the Smic is an increase added on top of the automatic revaluation: the last one dates from July 2012, with 0.6% added to the legal formula [9]. Going from 1,478 to 1,500 euros net would be a very modest gesture; it would remain far from the 100 to 150 euros asked by the CFDT and the CGT [1][3].

The decree mentioned aims at a knock-on effect: when the Smic rises, some sector minimums (the floor wages negotiated sector by sector) fall below the Smic; the government wants to push companies to raise them, which spreads the increase beyond workers paid the Smic alone [5][9].

The issue goes beyond the Smic: eight trade-union organisations warn about the fragility of the social pact [8], and Lecornu is also asking for a new effort on State spending for the 2027 budget [7]. Franceinfo judges that a conference of this kind hardly produces concrete decisions in a single day, and the unions must decide on the next steps of the mobilisation after the meeting [10].

If you are paid the Smic, going to 1,500 euros net would mean about twenty euros more per month, against the 100 euros requested by the CFDT [1][3]. If your sector has minimums close to the Smic, the decree could open a negotiation in your company [9]. If you run a small business, the payroll-charge issue raised by the Medef concerns you directly [1]. Nothing is decided at the time of writing: government announcements are expected after the meeting.

news.2026-11-09-france-budget-senat-secu: Palais du Luxembourg (Senate), Paris, France
Budget: the Senate
Budget: the Senate takes over the social security bill from Monday, and the government could rule by ordinance, a first

After the rejection of the 2027 budget in the National Assembly, the Senate takes up the social security budget on Monday 9 November, with a formal vote on 18 November; the State budget follows from 20 November to 9 December. If nothing is voted within the deadlines, the executive could act by ordinance, which would be a first [1][4][5].
The Senate is examining the 2027 social security financing bill (PLFSS) in plenary session from Monday 9 November, with a formal vote scheduled for 18 November [1][3].
The National Assembly had rejected the PLFSS on Friday 23 October; the State budget bill (PLF) was rejected on 4 November by a unanimous vote of MPs, 458 votes against and none in favour [3][4].

The constitutional deadline for the PLFSS expires on 26 November; the Senate examines the PLF from 20 November to 9 December, in its original version, and the compromise is pushed back to December [3][4][6].

The Senate's social affairs committee examined the text on 4 November; its chair, Philippe Mouiller, committed the committee to holding the deficit level set by the government, 12.7 billion euros [2].
For the PLF, the finance committee examines the articles of the first part on Thursday 12 November, led by rapporteur general Christine Lavarde [7].

If the texts are not adopted when the deadlines expire, after 26 November for social security and 17 December for the State budget, the government could implement the provisions by ordinance, which would be a first [5][3].

The government is counting on growth of 1.8% in 2027 and a public deficit of 5% of GDP, against 5.4% expected for 2026; the social security deficit is expected to reach 21.8 billion euros in 2026 [4][3].

Key point: the Assembly rejected everything, so it is the Senate, where the right and centre dominate, that now sets the line, and the government has little room left to obtain a compromise before December [4][5].

The two budgets do not carry the same weight: the State budget (PLF) sets taxes and State spending; the social security budget (PLFSS) sets what health insurance, family benefits and pensions spend. The Senate wants to "hold the deficit level" of the government, which means it looks for savings of the same size, not necessarily in the same places [2].

Using ordinances would change the method: the government would have the budget applied without a final vote by Parliament. According to Banque des Territoires, some adjustments voted by senators could be kept if the government uses article 49.3, but a priori not if it goes through an ordinance [2]. That is why the Senate weighs on the final content, even without the Assembly.

The figures explain what is at stake: a public deficit of 5% of GDP in 2027 against 5.4% in 2026, and a social security deficit of 21.8 billion euros in 2026, which forces choices on reimbursements, benefits or revenue [3][4].

The social security budget decides what health insurance reimburses, family aid and pension financing: Senate amendments can therefore affect you at the pharmacy, at the doctor's or in retirement. The State budget sets taxes and public spending. If the government goes through ordinances, the 2027 rules would be set without a new vote by MPs [5].

Black Sea: after nine ships hit by drones in October, Ursula von der Leyen travels to Romania and Bulgaria

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is in Bucharest on Monday 9 November, then in Varna, Bulgaria, on Tuesday 10. She comes after drones hit nine cargo ships and tankers off the two countries over 24 days in October, with at least 30 sailors dead or missing according to the AP [1][2][3].
Ursula von der Leyen is travelling to Romania and Bulgaria on 9 and 10 November to discuss Black Sea security [5][3].
In Bucharest on Monday 9 November, President Nicușor Dan receives her at Cotroceni Palace at 3:30 p.m., and she is due to meet Prime Minister Luca Niculescu [3].
In Varna on Tuesday 10 November, she meets Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and visits the Nikola Vaptsarov Naval Academy [3][4].
In October, over 24 days, aerial and naval drones hit nine cargo ships and tankers off Bulgaria and Romania; the AP counts at least 30 sailors dead or missing [1][2].

The Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged chemical tanker, was hit on 15 October near the mouth of the Danube: seven of its twelve crew members are missing, human remains were found aboard and Bulgarian prosecutors ordered DNA tests [8].
Romania blames Russia, while Bulgaria has not formally accused it; NATO has said it would deploy patrol aircraft, radars and drones to deter new attacks [1][2].
The two countries are developing a joint maritime security hub, focused on hybrid and cyber threats and on environmental protection [7].

Key point: it is no longer just ships burning in the Black Sea; civilian vessels are being hit off the coasts of two EU and NATO countries, and the visit by the Commission president is a sign that Brussels is taking it up [2][3].

The stakes are first of all economic: the Black Sea is a trade and oil route, and cargo ships hit within a few weeks raise the question of port protection, crew coverage and transport costs for shipowners. The Wine Trader, with seven of twelve sailors missing, shows that the human cost is already heavy [8].

MEP Victor Negrescu expects from the visit "a moment of concrete decisions for the security of our country and for European investment"; he cites the maritime security hub as the immediate priority [6][7]. It remains to be seen whether Brussels brings funds and means, or only statements.

Attribution is still debated: Romania points to Russia, Bulgaria remains cautious [1]. This difference in tone makes a common European response harder, while NATO is already sending surveillance assets [2].

If you are a French reader, the effect is indirect but real: the Black Sea is a route for grain, oil and goods that also pass through European ports, and the maritime insurance bill ends up in prices [2]. Von der Leyen's announcements on Tuesday in Varna will show whether the Union pays to protect this route [3].

Italy
Italy: the 2027 budget enters Parliament under fire, with 5 billion euros asked from banks and insurers

Italy's Parliament opens hearings on Giorgia Meloni's 2027 budget on Monday 9 November: the Court of Auditors, insurers and banks appear until Thursday 12, when Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti is heard. The government wants about 5 billion euros from banks and insurers; the Cisl and insurers protest [1][2][3].

Hearings on the 2027 budget law begin on Monday 9 November: the Court of Auditors at 2:30 p.m., the insurers' association Ania at 3:50 p.m., the banks' association Abi on Tuesday morning, then the Bank of Italy, the Parliamentary Budget Office and Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti on Thursday 12 November, at 4 p.m. [1][2].

To raise revenue, the government is asking about 5 billion euros from banks and insurers, according to Milano Finanza (some sources count more than 5.5 billion); Giorgetti calls the amount "sustainable" and "absorbable by the system" [3][6].

He admits, however, that there is no agreement with the banks: "An agreement among ourselves, not with the banks," he summed up; among the options is a rise in the corporate-tax (Ires) surcharge for the sector [4][6].
On income tax (Irpef), a cut for the middle class is in doubt; the measure with the most support is a cut for under-30s, and a cut for incomes above 50,000 euros remains ruled out for now [4][6].
The text is "under siege": the Cisl (a union) and insurers oppose it, the Regions judge the health funds insufficient and the opposition criticises the pensions chapter [5].
According to the observatory of economist Carlo Cottarelli, the tax burden would rise from 43% in 2026 to 43.2% in 2027 [5].
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni defends her minister, saying that "his rigour is also mine", while mentioning room for improvement in Parliament [1].
Key point: the Italian government has to finance its budget by asking banks for an effort rather than by raising household taxes, and this choice triggers a tight negotiation with the sector [3][4].

The mechanism: a budget law is first presented by the government, then amended by Parliament; hearings serve to listen to those who will pay or receive. If banks and insurers obtain relief, the 5 billion will have to be found elsewhere, which weighs on the Irpef and on pensions, two issues already in dispute [4][5].

The background figures show the constraint: if the tax burden rises from 43% to 43.2%, it means that, despite a targeted tax cut, the government is not managing to reduce the overall weight of levies [5]. The rigour displayed by Giorgetti and defended by Meloni aims at the country's financial credibility with the markets [1][2].

To watch: the text is not frozen; Meloni speaks of room for improvement in Parliament and the discussion on the Superbonus (a renovation subsidy) remains open, where Leo, from the government, has opened up to the Abi [1][5].

If you have an account or a loan with an Italian bank, or if you are insured in Italy, the tax on the sector may end up in fees, even though nothing is decided. For a French reader, this debate shows how a neighbouring State seeks revenue by making banks pay rather than households [3][6].

news.2026-11-09-allemagne-aigner-candida: Germany: Merz proposes Ilse Aigner for the federal presidency, a first for a woman

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has chosen Ilse Aigner, 61, a CSU politician, to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier. The election by the Federal Assembly is planned for 30 January 2027; the Linke criticises the method, and support will have to be widened beyond the coalition [1][2][3].
Ilse Aigner, 61, of the Bavarian CSU, is the Union's candidate for the federal presidency; Merz proposed her and the official nomination was expected this Monday 9 November [1][2].
The Federal Assembly (1,260 members, absolute majority at 631 votes) is due to vote on 30 January 2027 at the Reichstag; Steinmeier's second term ends in March 2027 [3].
Aigner would be the first woman in the post: the coalition leaders had agreed to propose a woman after twelve men [2][3].

The coalition's proposal is not enough on its own; according to Handelsblatt, Merz also wants to bring in the Greens, while views differ on the left: one article says the Linke and the AfD reject Aigner, another that the Linke has not decided [1][2].

Key point: it is a test of the solidity of Merz's black-red coalition, since one article reports that trust has eroded on both sides while another judges Aigner a good solution for the coalition as a whole [2].
The federal president has no governing power, but signs laws and nominates the chancellor; a candidate backed well beyond the coalition sends a signal of political stability abroad [1][3].
This does not change your life overnight, but it is an indicator of the stability of the government of the Union's largest economy, with which France negotiates the EU budget and defence.

news.2026-11-09-pays-bas-plan-fiscal-202: Netherlands: Rob Jetten's minority government stakes its 2027 tax plan on Thursday, ten seats short of a majority

Prime Minister Rob Jetten's minority cabinet puts its 2027 tax plan to a vote in the lower house on Thursday 12 November, without an agreement with the opposition. It is ten seats short and has already dropped one contribution and postponed a VAT increase to attract votes [1][2][3].

The Jetten cabinet adjusted its tax plan in an extraordinary council of ministers: it drops the "vrijheidsbijdrage" for 2027 and postpones the VAT increase on ornamental plants; the purchasing-power package is improved by 1.5 billion euros according to the Prime Minister [2].
The cabinet is ten seats short in the lower house; a majority seems possible with ChristenUnie, 50Plus and the Markuszower group [3].
On Wednesday evening, Pro and Volt offered to help, on condition that the wealth tax raises 1.5 billion euros more; its partner VVD is strongly opposed [3].
The plan must also pass the upper house before the end of the year; the BBB has eleven senators there for three seats in the lower house [3].
Key point: a government without a majority has to buy every vote, and every concession on purchasing power or taxation is paid for elsewhere in the budget [2][3].
The calendar is tight: according to EenVandaag, the tax administration locks its systems on 20 November, which can complicate implementation if the vote is delayed [1].
If you work or invest in the Netherlands, the tax plan sets 2027 taxes, including household purchasing power. For a French reader, it is an example of a minority government negotiating text by text.

news.2026-11-09-pologne-rpp-taux-inflati: Poland: the central bank keeps its rate at 3.75%, inflation falls back to 3.5%, but a rate rise remains possible in 2027

Poland's Monetary Policy Council left its key rate at 3.75% at its 3–4 November meeting, while October inflation fell back to 3.5% year on year from 4.1% in September. Part of the drop comes from a scheme that ends in late 2026 [1][2].
The Monetary Policy Council (RPP) kept the reference rate at 3.75%, the Lombard rate at 4.25% and the deposit rate at 3.25% [1].

Inflation fell to 3.5% year on year in October, from 4.1% in September; according to StockWatch, part of the drop comes from a scheme called CPN, which is only meant to last until the end of the year [1].
Eighteen of the nineteen economists polled by the PAP agency expected no change; mBank economists judged a 0.25-point rise more likely [2].
A Port analyst expects no change before the end of 2026 but does not rule out a rise in early 2027, depending on oil and the zloty; the 3-month WIBOR rate was 3.92% on 2 November [1][2].
Key point: the fall in inflation is partly temporary, because it depends on a measure that ends in late 2026, so the central bank remains cautious [1].
For Poland, the largest country in Central Europe, the oil price and the value of the zloty weigh on its decisions, which ties it to the tensions in the Gulf [1].
If you have a loan in zlotys or export to Poland, the 3.75% rate and a possible rise in early 2027 matter for the price of money. This decision dates from 4 November.
